lesson.title: Multiplying a 3-Digit Number by a 1-Digit Number
lesson.subject: math

contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you multiplied 2-digit numbers using the area model. Today, the exact same method works on a 3-digit number — you just break it into one more piece.

Let's multiply 234 x 5. Break 234 into 200 + 30 + 4. Multiply each part by 5 separately: 200 x 5 = 1,000, 30 x 5 = 150, and 4 x 5 = 20. Add all three results together: 1,000 + 150 + 20 = 1,170. Same idea as yesterday — just one more piece to add.
Try it yourself with 316 x 4: break 316 into 300 + 10 + 6, multiply each part by 4, then add the three results. This same technique will keep working no matter how many digits a number has.

objectives: Multiply a 3-digit number by a 1-digit number using the area model/distributive property
Recognize that the same technique from 2-digit multiplication extends directly to 3-digit numbers
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's 2-digit x 1-digit area-model technique.
2. Work through 234 x 5 together, breaking it into 200+30+4.
3. Have the child try 316 x 4 independently, checking each partial product before summing.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's topic: 2-digit x 2-digit multiplication.
differentiationTips: Struggling: write out the place-value breakdown (200+30+4) for them before asking them to multiply each part
Ready for more: try a 4-digit x 1-digit problem to confirm the pattern keeps extending
Encourage estimating first (234 is close to 200, so the answer should be a bit more than 200x5=1,000) as a reasonableness check
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly extends Common Core Grade 4 Number & Operations in Base Ten (4.NBT.5, multiplying a multi-digit number by a one-digit number) from 2 digits to 3 digits, matching the unit's own area-model approach.

generationData.instructions: Use the area model (break the 3-digit number into hundreds, tens, and ones) to solve each problem.
